motivation: To characterize when a variety or quasivariety is generated by its free algebras in the infinitary sense, and to understand the relationship between structural completeness and tabularity.
method: The paper uses algebraic methods, including congruence meet-semidistributivity, the congruence extension property (CEP), and the concept of irreducible algebras, to prove criteria for strong structural completeness.
result: It proves that every quasivariety of finite type with CEP generated by finite algebras containing an infinite irreducible algebra is not strongly structurally complete, and that congruence meet-semidistributive varieties of finite type generated by finite algebras are strongly structurally complete iff they are tabular.
conclusion: Dummett's and Medvedev's logics are structurally complete but not strongly structurally complete; the paper also provides criteria for strong primitivity.

title: Black-Box Inference Of Llm Architectural Properties With Restrictive Api Access
authors: Christopher Ellis, Shreyas Chaudhari, Mei-Yu Wang, Leighton Barnes, Giulia Fanti, Jos\'e M. F. Moura
abstract: ArXiv:2607.01313v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In practice, most commercial LLM providers do not publicly release details of underlying LLM architectures. However, prior work has shown that given limited API access to an LLM (namely, top-[MATH] logits and/or a logit bias function), one can recover certain architectural details of an LLM, such as the hidden dimension of the feed-forward network. Perhaps in response to these results, most commercial LLM providers have restricted their APIs to expose only the single logit for each decoded token, and they no longer give users the ability to bias logits. We show that even under current restrictive APIs, several architectural parameters are still recoverable. We present NightVision, an attack that uses restrictive black-box API access to estimate the hidden dimension, depth, and parameter count of an LLM. Algorithmically, NightVision relies on a novel common set prompting technique in which multiple prompts expose log probabilities for the same set of output tokens; a spectral analysis of these results is used to infer hidden dimension. NightVision additionally uses end-to-end time to first token (TTFT) measurements and the estimated hidden dimension to estimate depth and parameter count. We empirically evaluate NightVision on 32 open-source LLMs, recovering hidden dimension to within 23% average relative error across all models (9% on MoE models), and depth and parameter count to within 53% for models exceeding three billion parameters. We run extensive ablations to demonstrate how these accuracies scale with token budget and model properties. Overall, our results suggest that current LLM APIs are not sufficiently restricted to fully obfuscate the architectural details of their underlying models.
tldr: This paper presents a method to infer architectural parameters of LLMs under restrictive API access using spectral analysis of log probabilities and time-to-first-token measurements.
motivation: Commercial LLM providers restrict API access to hide architectural details, but prior work showed recovery under less restrictive APIs. This work aims to recover such details even under current restrictive APIs.
method: NightVision uses a common set prompting technique to collect log probabilities for the same output tokens across multiple prompts, applies spectral analysis to estimate hidden dimension, and combines with TTFT measurements to estimate depth and parameter count.
result: On 32 open-source LLMs, hidden dimension is recovered within 23% average relative error (9% for MoE models), and depth and parameter count within 53% for models >3B parameters.
conclusion: Current LLM APIs are insufficient to fully obfuscate architectural details, as key parameters can still be inferred with reasonable accuracy.

title: Insights From GitHub Community On The Matter Standard: Developer Perspectives And Challenges
authors: Muhammad Hassan, Carl Gunter, Susan Landau, Masooda Bashir
abstract: ArXiv:2607.01494v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Matter seeks to resolve longstanding interoperability problems in the Internet of Things (IoT), yet little is known about how developers experience the standard in day to day work. This paper examines over 13,000 issues from the official Project CHIP GitHub repository to understand the kinds of problems contributors report when implementing and integrating Matter. Using topic modeling and qualitative analysis, we identify four recurring areas of concern, Testing, Interoperability, Development, and Platform and Network, and describe how they manifest in the evolution of the codebase and tooling. The findings reveal systematic technical and integration challenges and point to concrete opportunities to refine Matter's test infrastructure, cross vendor guidance, and documentation as the standard continues to mature.
tldr: This paper analyzes developer challenges in implementing the Matter IoT standard using GitHub issue data.
motivation: Understanding developer experiences with the Matter standard to improve its adoption and tooling.
method: Topic modeling and qualitative analysis of over 13,000 GitHub issues from the Project CHIP repository.
result: Identified four recurring areas of concern: Testing, Interoperability, Development, and Platform and Network.
conclusion: The findings highlight systematic technical and integration challenges, suggesting improvements for test infrastructure, cross-vendor guidance, and documentation.

title: Kani: A Model Checker For Rust
authors: R\'emi Delmas, Zyad Hassan, Qinheping Hu, Rahul Kumar, Felipe R. Monteiro, Thanh Nguyen, Adri\'an Palacios, Celina Val, Michael Tautschnig, Justus Adam, Daniel Schwartz-Narbonne, Carolyn Zech
abstract: ArXiv:2607.01504v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Rust's ownership type system prevents memory errors in safe code, but certain desirable properties remain orthogonal to compilation: the soundness of unsafe operations (e.g., raw pointer dereferences), functional correctness, and absence of runtime panics. We present Kani, an open-source model checker for Rust that pushes bounded model checking beyond bug-finding to provide correctness guarantees for these properties. Kani compiles proof harnesses from Rust's Mid-level Intermediate Representation (MIR) into CBMC's bit-precise verification engine, automatically checking a comprehensive set of safety properties with no user annotation. To extend verification from bounded to unbounded, Kani provides a specification language comprising function contracts, loop contracts, quantifiers, and function stubbing. We demonstrate feasibility through case studies on industrial Rust projects, where contracts upgraded verification from panic-freedom to functional correctness, uncovering six previously unknown bugs. Kani operates at scale in production CI, with over 16,000 harnesses verified per code change in the Rust standard library verification campaign.
tldr: Kani is a model checker for Rust that verifies safety properties and functional correctness using bounded model checking.
motivation: Rust's type system prevents memory errors in safe code, but unsafe operations, functional correctness, and absence of panics require additional verification.
method: Kani compiles proof harnesses from Rust's MIR into CBMC's bit-precise verification engine and provides a specification language with contracts, loop contracts, quantifiers, and stubbing.
result: Case studies on industrial Rust projects uncovered six previously unknown bugs and upgraded verification from panic-freedom to functional correctness.
conclusion: Kani demonstrates that bounded model checking can provide correctness guarantees for Rust at scale in production CI.

title: Janus: A Playground For User-Involved Agentic Permission Management
authors: Natalie Grace Brigham, Eugene Bagdasarian, Tadayoshi Kohno, Franziska Roesner
abstract: ArXiv:2607.01510v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: AI agents that autonomously execute tool calls on a user's behalf raise pressing questions about permission management: what role could users play, and what role should they play? Despite many proposed approaches, the user's role in agentic permission management remains under explored. We introduce Janus, a playground system for implementing and evaluating user-involved agentic permission management designs. Janus consists of two components: Janus-Core, a modular agentic system supporting a diverse spectrum of permission management designs, and Janus-Harness, an automated evaluation framework. Grounded in a conceptual model that identifies key design axes for user involvement, we implement six permission assistants spanning the design space and evaluate them across three scenarios and three synthetic responders. We demonstrate that user input is critical and can significantly strengthen privacy and security, that AI augmentation of user decisions can help reduce cognitive load, and that realistic user behavior including permission fatigue must be accounted for in system design. No single design performs optimally across all contexts, motivating a more principled and context-sensitive approach to deploying permission assistants in agentic systems. Janus is publicly available to support future investigation into this dimension of agentic system design.
tldr: This paper presents Janus, a playground system for designing and evaluating user-involved permission management for AI agents.
motivation: The role of users in agentic permission management is underexplored, and there is a need for systematic evaluation of different design approaches.
method: The authors built Janus-Core, a modular agentic system supporting various permission management designs, and Janus-Harness, an automated evaluation framework. They implemented six permission assistants and tested them across three scenarios with synthetic responders.
result: User input significantly strengthens privacy and security; AI augmentation reduces cognitive load; realistic user behavior like permission fatigue must be considered; no single design is optimal across all contexts.
conclusion: A principled, context-sensitive approach is needed for deploying permission assistants in agentic systems.

title: Asymmetric Trading Prophets
authors: Gagan Aggarwal, Anupam Gupta, Yifan Wang, Mingfei Zhao
abstract: ArXiv:2607.01516v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The "Trading Prophet" problem challenges an online trader to maximize its profit by buying and selling assets under stochastic prices and capacity constraints, competing against an offline prophet with full foresight. In previous work, each arriving asset was assumed to have a single price [MATH], and the trader was allowed to either buy a copy at this price (subject to having available capacity), or sell a copy (if it already held at least one copy in hand). However, this abstraction can fail to capture the structural asymmetry of decentralized dealer-based markets, where buying and selling opportunities could be distinct, and driven by individual preferences. To address this, we introduce the Asymmetric Trading Prophets problem, where at each timestep the trader observes a price tuple [MATH] -- representing the cost to buy, and the revenue from selling at this timestep. Importantly, the [MATH] tuple could be potentially arbitrarily correlated. We provide the first competitive analysis for this asymmetric trading prophets problem, characterizing the achievable profit based on the trader's capacity [MATH] and initial inventory [MATH]. For the unit-capacity case of [MATH], we design online algorithms that achieve constant competitive ratios for both i.i.d. and non-i.i.d. distributions on the price tuples, when the trader has one initial copy ([MATH]). For the general capacity case where [MATH] can be large, we give algorithms for i.i.d. distributions that achieve a competitive ratio of [MATH]. Finally, for the symmetric case (where the price tuple satisfies [MATH]), we improve this to get a competitive ratio of [MATH], demonstrating that the performance approaches optimality as the capacity increases. We show that both ratios are tight up to a logarithmic factor.
tldr: This paper studies an online trading problem with asymmetric buy and sell prices, providing competitive analysis against an offline prophet.
motivation: Previous trading prophet models assume a single price per asset, which fails to capture the asymmetry in decentralized dealer-based markets where buying and selling opportunities are distinct.
method: The authors introduce the Asymmetric Trading Prophets problem, design online algorithms for unit-capacity and general capacity cases under i.i.d. and non-i.i.d. price distributions, and prove competitive ratios.
result: For unit capacity, constant competitive ratios are achieved. For general capacity, a competitive ratio of O(log K) is obtained for i.i.d. distributions, and for symmetric prices, the ratio improves to O(1) approaching optimality as capacity increases.
conclusion: The paper provides the first competitive analysis for asymmetric trading prophets, with tight bounds up to logarithmic factors, demonstrating that performance approaches optimality with larger capacity.

title: AgentFlow: Building Agent Dependency Graphs For Static Analysis Of Agent Programs
authors: Shenao Wang, Xinyi Hou, Yanjie Zhao, Xiao Cheng, Haoyu Wang
abstract: ArXiv:2607.01640v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: LLM agents are increasingly developed as source-code applications built on agent frameworks. These agent programs combine conventional host-language code with framework-defined semantics for models, prompts, tools, memory, and multi-agent orchestration logic. As a result, their behavior depends not only on traditional control and data flows, but also on a new class of agent dependencies. Such dependencies are often expressed as framework-induced semantics, such as agent constructors, tool decorators, and agent handoff declarations, making them difficult to recover with existing static analysis or dependency tracking tools. In this paper, we present AgentFlow, the first static analysis framework for recovering and analyzing agent dependencies from agent programs. AgentFlow constructs an Agent Dependency Graph (ADG), a framework-agnostic graph representation that represents agents, prompts, models, capabilities, memory states, and control policies as typed nodes, and captures their component-dependency, control-flow, and data-flow dependencies as typed edges. Built on ADGs, AgentFlow supports a range of analyses for agent governance and security, including Agent Bill of Materials (BOM) generation and prompt-to-tool risk detection. We implement AgentFlow for five representative agent frameworks and evaluate it on AgentZoo, a corpus of 5,399 real-world agent programs. Our evaluation shows that AgentFlow recovers richer agent entities and dependencies than existing AST-based agent static analysis tools, generates more dependency-aware Agent BOMs, and uncovers 238 taint-style prompt-to-tool risks in real-world agent programs. These results show that ADG provides a practical foundation for understanding, governing, and securing emerging agent software.
tldr: AgentFlow is a static analysis framework for LLM agent programs that constructs Agent Dependency Graphs to recover agent-specific dependencies for governance and security.
motivation: LLM agent programs combine conventional code with framework-defined semantics, creating agent dependencies that existing static analysis tools cannot recover.
method: AgentFlow builds a framework-agnostic Agent Dependency Graph (ADG) with typed nodes and edges representing agents, prompts, models, tools, memory, and control flows, and implements analyses like Agent BOM generation and prompt-to-tool risk detection.
result: Evaluated on 5,399 real-world agent programs across five frameworks, AgentFlow recovers richer dependencies than existing tools, generates more comprehensive Agent BOMs, and uncovers 238 taint-style prompt-to-tool risks.
conclusion: ADG provides a practical foundation for understanding, governing, and securing emerging agent software.

title: Expander Sparse Autoencoders: Parameter-Efficient Dictionaries For Mechanistic Interpretability
authors: Rodrigo Mendoza-Smith
abstract: ArXiv:2607.01799v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) decompose internal activations of neural networks into sparse linear combinations of learned features by fitting an overcomplete dictionary [MATH] with [MATH], and inferring a sparse code [MATH] from [MATH]. This inference problem closely resembles the canonical setup of compressed sensing, but dense decoders requires [MATH] learned values, which becomes costly at large feature counts. We introduce Expander SAEs: TopK SAEs whose decoder and tied encoder are supported on a left-[MATH]-regular expander mask with [MATH], learning only [MATH] decoder values while keeping the sparse-coding problem [MATH] fixed. The same structure reduces storage and turns the matching-pursuit correlation step [MATH] in OMP into an [MATH] gather-and-reduce operation. Our experiments show that across Pythia-70M/160M, Qwen2.5-3B, and Llama-3.2-1B residual-stream activations, varying [MATH] traces a consistent storage--fidelity frontier, and that at the most compressed modern-LM setting, Qwen2.5-3B with [MATH] uses [MATH] fewer learned decoder values than the full dense decoder while retaining [MATH]% of dense CE-loss recovered. Control experiments show that the improved storage--fidelity tradeoff is driven by sparse, diverse decoder support structure rather than by fewer learned decoder values, and that when sparse and dense decoders are compared at matched parameter count, part of the remaining gap comes from encoder amortisation. On the theoretical side, we show that expansion and column flatness are sufficient for identifiability of noiseless [MATH]-sparse codes, and we derive complementary sufficient conditions under which OMP recovers the support exactly.
tldr: This paper introduces Expander Sparse Autoencoders, a parameter-efficient dictionary learning method for mechanistic interpretability of neural networks.
motivation: Standard sparse autoencoders require large learned dictionaries, which become costly at large feature counts. The authors aim to reduce storage and computational cost while maintaining fidelity.
method: They propose Expander SAEs, which use a left-regular expander mask to sparsify the decoder and tied encoder, reducing the number of learned parameters and enabling efficient gather-and-reduce operations in matching pursuit.
result: Experiments on various language models show that Expander SAEs achieve a consistent storage-fidelity frontier, using significantly fewer parameters while retaining most of the cross-entropy loss recovery. Theoretical results show expansion and column flatness suffice for identifiability of sparse codes.
conclusion: Expander SAEs offer a practical way to scale sparse autoencoders to large feature counts with reduced memory and compute, with theoretical guarantees on sparse code recovery.

title: Congestion-Based Slot Pricing In A Railway Auction Game
authors: Sebastiaan Meijer Bill Roungas
abstract: ArXiv:2607.01822v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We present a multi-agent system for studying the allocation of discrete, congested resources among heterogeneous strategic agents, motivated by the problem of railway slot allocation under deregulation. Multiple operator-agents, differing in size and capacity, interact through a shared auction mechanism over repeated rounds under time-constrained decision-making. The mechanism combines a congestion-based base price that increases with aggregate demand with an asymmetric corrective adjustment that penalises the agent requesting the most slots and rewards the agent requesting the fewest, and is designed to mitigate strategic dominance by large agents while preserving transparency and congestion sensitivity. We formulate the interaction as a repeated game with incomplete information and implement the system as a real-time, web-based multi-agent environment in which human participants control individual agents and observe live marginal-cost and competitor feedback. We report exploratory observations from two structured sessions with domain experts acting as operator-agents. The congestion mechanism responds to aggregate demand as designed and the corrective incentives are actively triggered, but agents representing large operators persist with high-request strategies despite the penalty, suggesting that corrective pricing is necessary but not sufficient to neutralise strategic dominance in this multi-agent setting. A post-session debrief indicates that participants' decisions were driven by the assumed agent role rather than personal disposition, and provides qualitative support for strategic motives, such as preserving market presence and raising rivals' costs, operating alongside short-term profit maximisation. We discuss implications for multi-agent mechanism design under asymmetric budgets and outline directions for analytical validation and larger-scale multi-agent experiments.
tldr: This paper studies a multi-agent railway slot allocation auction with congestion-based pricing, using a web-based experimental platform with human participants.
motivation: To design a fair and efficient mechanism for allocating congested railway slots among heterogeneous operators under deregulation, mitigating strategic dominance by large agents.
method: A repeated game with incomplete information is implemented as a real-time multi-agent environment; human participants act as operators and interact through an auction combining congestion-based base price and asymmetric corrective adjustment.
result: The congestion mechanism responds to demand and corrective incentives are triggered, but large operators persist with high-request strategies despite penalties, indicating corrective pricing alone is insufficient.
conclusion: The study suggests that corrective pricing is necessary but not sufficient to neutralize strategic dominance, and calls for analytical validation and larger-scale experiments.

title: ElephantAgent: Contextual State Continuity In Agentic Systems
authors: Jiankai Jin, Xiangzheng Zhang, Zhao Liu, Wenzhuo Xu, Dongdong Yang, Deyue Zhang, Quanchen Zou
abstract: ArXiv:2607.01919v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Agentic systems enhance their capabilities by invoking external tools and maintaining persistent memory. However, these external dependencies introduce novel attack surfaces. Recent tool and memory poisoning attacks show that maliciously crafted tool descriptors and poisoned memory can covertly bias agent behavior. These threats reflect a deeper issue: the lack of verifiable continuity in the agent's contextual state for planning and execution. We present ElephantAgent, a protocol that enforces Contextual State Continuity to defend against contextual state poisoning. Inspired by prior state-continuity mechanisms (e.g., Nimble), ElephantAgent extends this protection to the evolving contextual state of agentic systems. We define the contextual state as the bounded, security-critical subset of the agent's entire context (e.g., tool state and memory). Before processing each query, ElephantAgent recomputes the digest of the local contextual state and verifies it against the latest authorized digest. Using replicated trusted hardware, ElephantAgent maintains a linearizable ledger of authorized contextual state transitions and detects out-of-band state tampering. To handle in-band semantic abuse, ElephantAgent additionally provides Historical Traceability, enabling conditional post-hoc audit and recovery to a known-good prior state.
tldr: This paper proposes a protocol for ensuring contextual state continuity in agentic systems using trusted hardware and linearizable ledgers.
motivation: Agentic systems are vulnerable to tool and memory poisoning attacks that can covertly bias agent behavior due to lack of verifiable continuity in contextual state.
method: ElephantAgent recomputes a digest of the local contextual state before each query and verifies it against an authorized digest maintained on replicated trusted hardware, with a linearizable ledger of state transitions.
result: The protocol detects out-of-band state tampering and provides historical traceability for post-hoc audit and recovery.
conclusion: ElephantAgent enforces contextual state continuity to defend against poisoning attacks in agentic systems.

title: Towards A Phonology-Informed Evaluation Of Multilingual Tts
authors: Sneha Ray Barman, Neeraj Kumar Sharma, Shakuntala Mahanta
abstract: ArXiv:2607.01965v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Neural TTS systems can sound natural across languages, but naturalness does not guarantee the preservation of sound contrasts that distinguish words from their grammatical forms. Standard metrics like MOS do not test for this. We propose a classifier-based framework that audits TTS output against language-specific phonological patterns using human speech as a benchmark. Testing Assamese advanced tongue root (ATR) vowel harmony with Meta's MMS TTS, we show that a classifier trained on human speech transfers to synthesized speech with minimal loss. The faithfulness audit reveals that [+ATR] mid vowels are realized as [-ATR] in 1/3 tokens despite an underlying [+ATR] specification, a bias absent in human speech. At the word level, predicted ATR labels classify harmony more accurately than transcription labels, indicating a gap between intended and produced phonology. The framework offers task-specific diagnostics and generalizes to other phonological contrasts with measurable acoustic cues.
tldr: This paper proposes a phonology-informed evaluation framework for multilingual TTS, focusing on Assamese vowel harmony.
motivation: Standard metrics like MOS do not test whether TTS preserves sound contrasts that distinguish grammatical forms.
method: A classifier trained on human speech is used to audit TTS output against language-specific phonological patterns.
result: The audit reveals that [+ATR] mid vowels are realized as [-ATR] in 1/3 tokens, a bias absent in human speech.
conclusion: The framework offers task-specific diagnostics and generalizes to other phonological contrasts with measurable acoustic cues.

title: Fine-Grained Bounds For Courcelle's Theorem
authors: Daniel Lokshtanov, Fahad Panolan, Saket Saurabh, Jie Xue, Meirav Zehavi
abstract: ArXiv:2607.02033v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Courcelle's theorem states that there exists an algorithm that takes as input a graph [MATH] of treewidth at most [MATH] and a MSO formula [MATH], and determines whether [MATH] satisfies [MATH] in time [MATH]. It is folklore that the the function [MATH] contains a tower of exponentials whose height depends as a linear function of the number of quantifier alternations of the input formula [MATH]. A classic reduction of Frick and Grohe shows that, assuming the Exponential Time Hypothesis (ETH), the linear growth of the height of the tower is unavoidable. Nevertheless, there is still a huge gap between existing upper and lower bounds -- after all, there is quite a difference between a single exponential and a double exponential running time. In addition, this only gives us a very coarse understanding in the time complexity of Courcelle's theorem. In this paper, we prove a fine-grained version of Courcelle's theorem with nearly ETH-tight dependence on the treewidth parameter [MATH] and the quantifier structure of [MATH] (specifically, the number of first order and second order variables in each quantifier alternation block).
tldr: This paper proves fine-grained complexity bounds for Courcelle's theorem on graphs of bounded treewidth, with nearly tight dependence on treewidth and quantifier structure.

title: HaloGuard 1.0: An Open Weights Constitutional Classifier For Multilingual Ai Safety
authors: Navaneeth Sangameswaran, Preetham S, Ashmiya Lenin
abstract: ArXiv:2607.02079v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We present HaloGuard 1.0, an open-weights implementation of the constitutional-classifier paradigm for input safety. It achieves state-of-the-art performance on English and multilingual prompt-safety benchmarks at roughly one-tenth the model size of current leading open guard models. The safety constitution is the organising structure of the corpus: a natural-language constitution of 46 policies and 2,940 subcategories drives synthetic data generation, with exhaustive one-to-one paired counterfactuals that hold topic and vocabulary fixed while flipping intent, a two-tier harmless design that separately targets boundary and baseline false positives (FPs), and balanced multilingual materialisation across 46 languages that treats language as a surface form appearing on both sides of the boundary rather than as an adversarial signal. Across seven prompt-safety benchmarks, HaloGuard 1.0-0.8B attains the best average F1 (90.9) of any open guard we evaluate, outperforming baselines up to 27B parameters (over 30 times larger) while holding false-positive rate (FPR) to 4.3 and false-negative rate (FNR) to 9.5. The HaloGuard 1.0-4B variant reaches average F1 of 92.1 and FPR of 3.5, spending its extra capacity on precision rather than recall. A structured adjudication of the remaining failures indicates that most apparent missed-harm cases are benchmark mislabels rather than genuine model misses. An always-on adversarial red-teaming protocol continuously hardens the guard against both content-level and agentic attacks. We release the models as open weights.

conclusion: The model demonstrates that small, constitution-driven classifiers can match or exceed larger models in prompt safety, and continuous red-teaming further hardens the guard against attacks.

[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021031] Published Mon May 11, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies fatigue fracture in hydrogels using folded proteins as mechanically well-defined units, bridging single-molecule and bulk experiments.
motivation: Understanding fatigue fracture in soft materials is crucial for designing durable hydrogels, but the molecular mechanisms are poorly understood.
method: The authors use folded proteins as model units to probe mechanical fatigue at the single-molecule level and connect to bulk hydrogel behavior.
result: They develop a force-response model that explains fatigue behavior and provides design principles for fatigue-resistant hydrogels.
conclusion: The work offers a strategy for engineering hydrogels with improved fatigue resistance based on molecular-level insights.

title: Hydroplasticity Of Nanocrystal Films Induced By Mesopore Change
authors: Siyuan Liu, Yonggui Wang, Yu Yin, Xintong Meng, Zhen Lang, And Kai Zhang
abstract:
Author(s): Siyuan Liu, Yonggui Wang, Yu Yin, Xintong Meng, Zhen Lang, and Kai Zhang

A vapor training process allows for improved plasticity and better shaping of wood-derived films.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021026] Published Tue May 05, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies the hydroplasticity of nanocrystal films induced by mesopore change, a materials science topic unrelated to quantum information theory.
motivation: To improve the plasticity and shaping of wood-derived films through a vapor training process.
method: Experimental investigation of nanocrystal films and their mesopore structure changes under vapor treatment.
result: The vapor training process enhances plasticity and enables better shaping of the films.
conclusion: The findings advance the understanding of hydroplasticity in nanocrystal films, with potential applications in materials engineering.

title: Cell Bulging And Extrusion In A Three-Dimensional Bubbly Vertex Model For Curved Epithelial Sheets
authors: Oliver M. Drozdowski, Büşra Kocameşe-Tamgac𝚤, Kim E. Boonekamp, Michael Boutros, And Ulrich S. Schwarz
abstract:
Author(s): Oliver M. Drozdowski, Büşra Kocameşe-Tamgac𝚤, Kim E. Boonekamp, Michael Boutros, and Ulrich S. Schwarz

Cells at topological defects in curved epithelial sheets experience mechanical forces that facilitate extrusion.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021023] Published Thu Apr 30, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies cell bulging and extrusion in curved epithelial sheets using a three-dimensional bubbly vertex model.
motivation: Understanding how mechanical forces at topological defects drive cell extrusion in curved tissues is important for developmental biology and disease.
method: The authors develop a 3D bubbly vertex model to simulate epithelial sheets with curvature and analyze cell shape changes and extrusion events.
result: They find that curvature and topological defects enhance cell bulging and extrusion, providing a mechanical explanation for observed phenomena.
conclusion: The model reveals key mechanical principles governing cell dynamics in curved epithelia, with implications for tissue morphogenesis and homeostasis.

title: Seeing New Depths: Three-Dimensional Flow Of A Free-Swimming Alga
authors: Gregorius Pradipta, Wanho Lee, van Tran, Kyle Welch, Santosh K. Sankar, Yongsam Kim, Satish Kumar, Xin Yong, Jiarong Hong, Sookkyung Lim, And Xiang Cheng
abstract:
Author(s): Gregorius Pradipta, Wanho Lee, Van Tran, Kyle Welch, Santosh K. Sankar, Yongsam Kim, Satish Kumar, Xin Yong, Jiarong Hong, Sookkyung Lim, and Xiang Cheng

Experimental three-dimensional measurements of the flow field around a free-swimming microalga reveal that microscopic organisms generate unexpected low-Reynolds-number flow phenomena, expanding our understanding of microhydrodynamics with profound biological implications for microbial motility and physiology.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021019] Published Fri Apr 24, 2026.
tldr: This paper presents experimental 3D measurements of the flow field around a free-swimming microalga, revealing unexpected low-Reynolds-number flow phenomena.
motivation: Understanding the hydrodynamics of microbial motility is important for biology and microfluidics, but the paper does not connect to quantum information or thermodynamics.
method: The authors used experimental three-dimensional flow measurements to study a free-swimming microalga.
result: They discovered unexpected low-Reynolds-number flow phenomena that expand understanding of microhydrodynamics.
conclusion: The findings have biological implications for microbial motility and physiology, but are unrelated to the user's research interests.

title: High-energy Emission From The Galactic Center
authors: Andrea Goldwurm, Maïca Clavel, Stefano Gabici, And Régis Terrier
abstract:
Author(s): Andrea Goldwurm, Maïca Clavel, Stefano Gabici, and Régis Terrier

In this review, the authors provide a comprehensive multiwavelength view of high-energy emission from the center of our Galaxy. This region contains the closest supermassive black hole to us, which offers the best studied galactic nucleus in the Universe, with its quiescent emission and accretion contrasted by flaring activity. The Galactic Center also hosts diverse compact sources, plasma bubbles, and x-ray chimneys, altogether forming a dense interacting molecular zone—a gigantic powerhouse in the Milky Way.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 025006] Published Mon Jun 29, 2026.
tldr: A review of high-energy astrophysical emission from the Galactic Center, focusing on the supermassive black hole and surrounding structures.
motivation: To provide a comprehensive multiwavelength overview of the Galactic Center's high-energy phenomena, including the black hole's accretion and flares.
method: Review of observational data across multiple wavelengths (X-ray, gamma-ray, etc.) and theoretical models.
result: Summarizes the current understanding of the Galactic Center's high-energy emission, including quiescent and flaring states, plasma bubbles, and chimneys.
conclusion: The Galactic Center is a unique laboratory for studying high-energy astrophysical processes, with many open questions remaining.

title: Fundamentals Of Vacuum Breakdown In High-gradient Accelerator Structures
authors: Walter Wuensch, Sergio Calatroni, Flyura Djurabekova, Andreas Kyritsakis, And Yinon Ashkenazy
abstract:
Author(s): Walter Wuensch, Sergio Calatroni, Flyura Djurabekova, Andreas Kyritsakis, and Yinon Ashkenazy

Vacuum breakdown or arcing happens when a very strong electric field causes a metal surface in a vacuum to suddenly form plasma, allowing large electrical currents to flow. Breakdown can damage particle accelerators, fusion reactors, satellites, and x-ray devices, though it is useful in technologies like plasma thrusters. Scientists have studied this unpredictable and fast phenomenon for over a century. Recent advances in experiments and computer simulations now provide a coherent mechanistic picture: tiny surface defects, electrical stress, heat, and emitted particles interact in complex ways to trigger breakdowns. These insights could improve high-power technologies and make advanced accelerators more reliable and efficient.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 025004] Published Fri Jun 05, 2026.
tldr: This paper reviews the physics of vacuum breakdown in high-gradient accelerator structures, focusing on surface defects, electrical stress, and plasma formation.
motivation: Vacuum breakdown limits the performance of particle accelerators and other high-power devices; understanding its mechanism is crucial for improving reliability.
method: The authors synthesize experimental observations and computer simulations to build a coherent mechanistic picture of the breakdown process.
result: They identify that tiny surface defects, electrical stress, heat, and emitted particles interact in complex ways to trigger breakdowns.
conclusion: These insights could improve high-power technologies and make advanced accelerators more reliable and efficient.

title: Colloquium: Hadron Production In Open-charm Meson Pairs At ${e}^{+}{e}^{−}$ Colliders
authors: Xiongfei Wang, Xiang Liu, And Yuanning Gao
abstract:
Author(s): Xiongfei Wang, Xiang Liu, and Yuanning Gao

Hadron spectroscopy is a frontier of particle physics; searching for new hadrons is crucial for validating the theory of strong interaction (QCD). Investigating how charmonium, a bound state of charm and anticharm quarks, decays and searching for new charmoniumlike states yield valuable insights into strong interaction mechanisms, including quark confinement and gluon binding. Hadrons produced at e− collisions decaying to open-charm meson pairs are a primary source of experimental information for these investigations. This Colloquium reviews current progress from BARBAR, Belle, CLEO-c, and BESIII experiments. As BESIII accumulates high-precision data, it has emerged as the leading facility for measuring hadron production in charm-meson pair systems, and recent advances are highlighted.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 021001] Published Fri Apr 03, 2026.
tldr: This Colloquium reviews hadron production in open-charm meson pairs at e+e- colliders, focusing on charmonium decays and new hadron searches.
motivation: Understanding strong interaction mechanisms such as quark confinement and gluon binding through charmonium decays and searches for new charmoniumlike states.
method: Review of experimental progress from BaBar, Belle, CLEO-c, and BESIII experiments, highlighting recent advances from BESIII.
result: Summarizes current knowledge and recent high-precision data on hadron production in charm-meson pair systems.
conclusion: BESIII has emerged as the leading facility for such measurements, providing valuable insights into QCD.

title: Editorial: A Tribute To The Arecibo Observatory
authors: Véronique van Elewyck And Dietrich Belitz
abstract:
Author(s): Véronique Van Elewyck and Dietrich Belitz

Three Colloquia honor the Arecibo Observatory’s legacy, exploring its revolutionary impact on planetary radar studies, radio astronomy, and geospace science.

[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 010001] Published Tue Mar 31, 2026.
tldr: An editorial tribute to the Arecibo Observatory, summarizing its contributions to planetary radar, radio astronomy, and geospace science.
motivation: To honor the legacy of the Arecibo Observatory and its impact on multiple scientific fields.
method: The paper is an editorial that reviews the observatory's achievements through three colloquia.
result: Highlights the observatory's revolutionary contributions to planetary radar studies, radio astronomy, and geospace science.
conclusion: The Arecibo Observatory had a profound and lasting impact on science, and its legacy is celebrated.

title: Colloquium: Planetary Radar At The Arecibo Observatory
authors: Michael C. Nolan, Lynn M. Carter, And Edgard G. Rivera-Valentín
abstract:
Author(s): Michael C. Nolan, Lynn M. Carter, and Edgard G. Rivera-Valentín

For more than two decades, the planetary radar installed at the Arecibo Telescope was the most sensitive instrument of its kind, harnessing the penetrating power of radio waves to perform observations of the (sub)surface of planets, moons, and asteroids in the Solar System—providing a unique perspective on those bodies that helped to drive in situ exploration. This Colloquium presents an overview of the scientific legacy of the Arecibo radar system, focusing on the period posterior to the Gregorian Update in the late 1990s until the unexpected demise of the telescope in 2020. After recalling the basics of planetary radar techniques, it reviews key Arecibo observations of Mercury, Venus, Mars, our Moon, and the Saturn system, and highlights its essential role in the characterization of a large sample of near-Earth asteroids and comets.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 011003] Published Tue Mar 31, 2026.
tldr: This colloquium reviews the scientific legacy of planetary radar observations at the Arecibo Observatory, focusing on Solar System bodies.
motivation: Planetary radar provides unique subsurface and surface information about planets, moons, and asteroids, complementing in situ exploration.
method: The paper summarizes radar techniques and reviews key Arecibo observations of Mercury, Venus, Mars, the Moon, the Saturn system, and near-Earth asteroids and comets.
result: Arecibo's radar system was the most sensitive of its kind, enabling detailed characterization of Solar System objects and supporting planetary science.
conclusion: The Arecibo radar system made significant contributions to planetary science, and its loss marks the end of an era for ground-based planetary radar.

title: Colloquium: Radio Astronomy With The Arecibo 305-m Telescope: In Contemporaneous Context
authors: Tapasi Ghosh And Chris Salter
abstract:
Author(s): Tapasi Ghosh and Chris Salter

The Arecibo Observatory, inaugurated in 1963 as the world’s largest single-dish radio telescope, remained at the forefront of astronomy and atmospheric science for more than five decades, until its catastrophic collapse in December 2020. This Colloquium focuses on Arecibo’s enduring legacy in radio astronomy, offering a historical perspective that emphasizes how successive major upgrades of the telescope continuously expanded its observational capabilities and scientific impact. It presents Arecibo’s most influential contributions in topics as diverse as pulsar studies, the mapping of neutral hydrogen (HI) in the Milky Way and other galaxies, the characterization of the interstellar medium, the imaging of extragalactic radio sources with very long baseline interferometry (VLBI), the search for extraterrestrial intelligence (SETI), and being a major contributor to the first-ever detection of a stochastic gravitational-wave background.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 011004] Published Tue Mar 31, 2026.
tldr: This paper reviews the history and scientific legacy of the Arecibo 305-m radio telescope, covering its contributions to radio astronomy and atmospheric science.
motivation: To provide a historical perspective on Arecibo's impact and to document its major scientific achievements before its collapse.
method: The paper is a colloquium-style review, summarizing key upgrades and observational milestones across decades.
result: Arecibo enabled breakthroughs in pulsar studies, HI mapping, VLBI, SETI, and gravitational-wave detection.
conclusion: Arecibo's legacy endures through its transformative contributions to radio astronomy and its role in inspiring future facilities.

title: Colloquium: Geospace Pathfinder Science At Arecibo Observatory
authors: J. D. Mathews, M. P. Sulzer, And Shikha Raizada
abstract:
Author(s): J. D. Mathews, M. P. Sulzer, and Shikha Raizada

The Arecibo Observatory housed the largest single-aperture radio telescope for approximately 50 years. A major scientific focus was studying the upper atmosphere; its highly sensitive radar facility, combined with lidars, optical sensors, and satellite-based systems, enabled unprecedented studies of ionospheric physics based on incoherent scattering of radio waves off free electrons. After establishing the fundamental concepts and observables of the incoherent scattering radar technique, this Colloquium reviews key advances obtained with the Arecibo suite of instruments in multiple areas of geospace science, including plasma physics, space weather, lidar studies of atomic metals in the ionosphere, and ionosphere-magnetosphere coupling.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 011005] Published Tue Mar 31, 2026.
tldr: This paper reviews geospace science advances made using the Arecibo Observatory's radar and lidar instruments, focusing on ionospheric physics and space weather.
motivation: The Arecibo Observatory's unique capabilities for studying the upper atmosphere have enabled significant advances in geospace science, and this Colloquium aims to summarize those contributions.
method: The paper reviews the incoherent scatter radar technique and presents key results from Arecibo's suite of instruments, including lidars and optical sensors, in studies of plasma physics, space weather, and ionosphere-magnetosphere coupling.
result: The review highlights advances in understanding ionospheric dynamics, atomic metal layers, and coupling processes between the ionosphere and magnetosphere.
conclusion: The Arecibo Observatory has been instrumental in advancing geospace science, and its legacy continues through the data and insights obtained over its operational lifetime.

title: Colloquium: Convection-cloud Chambers: Experiment And Theory
authors: Steven Krueger And Raymond A. Shaw
abstract:
Author(s): Steven Krueger and Raymond A. Shaw

In warm clouds, drops grow into raindrops through both condensation and collision coalescence, but the observed rapid transition between these mechanisms remains difficult to theoretically explain. The convection-cloud chamber, which reproduces key phenomena such as turbulent fluctuations in droplet concentrations and supersaturation under controlled laboratory conditions, offers a promising approach to addressing this long-standing bottleneck in understanding in cloud physics. This Colloquium reviews the physics underlying the precipitation bottleneck, examines how convection-cloud chambers capture the essential processes, and synthesizes insights from experiments, theory, and computational models that bridge laboratory and atmospheric scales.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 011001] Published Wed Feb 04, 2026.
tldr: This paper reviews convection-cloud chambers as a laboratory tool to study the precipitation bottleneck in warm clouds.
motivation: Understanding the rapid transition from condensation to collision-coalescence in warm clouds is a long-standing problem in cloud physics.
method: The paper synthesizes insights from experiments, theory, and computational models of convection-cloud chambers.
result: Convection-cloud chambers reproduce key phenomena such as turbulent fluctuations in droplet concentrations and supersaturation, offering a controlled environment to study the bottleneck.
conclusion: The convection-cloud chamber is a promising approach to bridge laboratory and atmospheric scales for understanding precipitation formation.

title: Colloquium: Gravitational Waves From Neutrino-driven Core Collapse Supernovae
authors: A. Mezzacappa And M. Zanolin
abstract:
Author(s): A. Mezzacappa and M. Zanolin

The observation of a core collapse supernova explosion of (near-)Galactic origin would constitute a landmark, once-in-a-century event for multimessenger astronomy, eagerly awaited by observers and modelers alike. The detection of gravitational waves, along with photons and neutrinos, from such an event would provide unique insights into the supernova central engine and the physics of the newly forming neutron star. This Colloquium presents the latest progress in core collapse supernova modeling and the associated gravitational wave signal predictions. It also provides an overview of the specific methods of detection and physical parameter estimation that can be implemented for such signals in ground-based laser interferometers, in the context of multimessenger research strategies.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 041002] Published Tue Dec 30, 2025.
tldr: This colloquium reviews gravitational wave signals from core collapse supernovae and their detection methods.
motivation: Observing a Galactic core collapse supernova would be a landmark event for multimessenger astronomy, providing insights into the supernova engine and neutron star physics.
method: The paper summarizes recent progress in supernova modeling and gravitational wave signal predictions, and discusses detection and parameter estimation techniques for ground-based laser interferometers.
result: The review presents the current state of gravitational wave predictions from core collapse supernovae and outlines multimessenger observation strategies.
conclusion: Gravitational wave detection from a nearby supernova, combined with photon and neutrino observations, will offer unique insights into the explosion mechanism and neutron star formation.

title: Colloquium: The Cosmic Dipole Anomaly
authors: Nathan Secrest, Sebastian von Hausegger, Mohamed Rameez, Roya Mohayaee, And Subir Sarkar
abstract:
Author(s): Nathan Secrest, Sebastian von Hausegger, Mohamed Rameez, Roya Mohayaee, and Subir Sarkar

The cosmological principle, which states that the Universe must be statistically isotropic and homogeneous on large scales, is a foundational principle of the standard model of cosmology, known as lambda cold dark matter (ΛCDM). The validity of this principle can be tested by assessing the compatibility of a dipole anisotropy in the large-scale distribution of matter with the dipole observed in the cosmic microwave background, interpreted in the ΛCDM model as due to our local peculiar motion. This Colloquium describes the methodology for such a test and presents its outcome based on the analysis of recent large catalogs of radio galaxies and quasars, revealing a significant inconsistency between the two dipoles. The authors review these recent findings, as well as potential biases, systematic issues, and alternate interpretations, and discuss how this anomaly could challenge the standard description of our Universe based on the ΛCDM model.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 041001] Published Thu Dec 11, 2025.
tldr: This paper reviews the cosmic dipole anomaly, a potential challenge to the cosmological principle and ΛCDM model, based on large-scale structure surveys.
motivation: To test the cosmological principle by comparing the dipole anisotropy in the distribution of radio galaxies and quasars with the CMB dipole.
method: Analysis of large catalogs of radio galaxies and quasars to measure the dipole in the matter distribution and compare it with the CMB dipole.
result: A significant inconsistency is found between the two dipoles, challenging the standard ΛCDM interpretation.
conclusion: The cosmic dipole anomaly may indicate a violation of the cosmological principle or require new physics beyond ΛCDM.

title: Astrophysical Tests Of Dark Matter Self-interactions
authors: Susmita Adhikari, Arka Banerjee, Kimberly K. Boddy, Francis-Yan Cyr-Racine, Harry Desmond, Cora Dvorkin, Bhuvnesh Jain, Felix Kahlhoefer, Manoj Kaplinghat, Anna Nierenberg, Annika H. G. Peter, Andrew Robertson, Jeremy Sakstein, And Jesús Zavala
abstract:
Author(s): Susmita Adhikari, Arka Banerjee, Kimberly K. Boddy, Francis-Yan Cyr-Racine, Harry Desmond, Cora Dvorkin, Bhuvnesh Jain, Felix Kahlhoefer, Manoj Kaplinghat, Anna Nierenberg, Annika H. G. Peter, Andrew Robertson, Jeremy Sakstein, and Jesús Zavala

Dark sectors, involving new particles that couple very weakly to the standard model ones, play an important role in current model-building efforts in particle physics, as they allow, for example, for new dark matter production and interaction mechanisms. This review focuses on self-interacting dark matter scenarios, their implications on the dynamics and distribution of dark matter halos in the Universe, and the related astrophysical tests and observations, from galaxies to large-scale structures. It is embedded in the framework of the Novel Probes Project, a forum connecting observers and theorists involved in the study of astrophysical tests of dark-sector interactions.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 045004] Published Mon Dec 08, 2025.
tldr: This paper reviews astrophysical tests of dark matter self-interactions, focusing on dark sector models and their observational signatures.
motivation: To understand the nature of dark matter by testing self-interacting dark matter scenarios against astrophysical observations.
method: The paper is a review that synthesizes theoretical predictions and observational constraints from galaxies to large-scale structures.
result: It summarizes current constraints on dark matter self-interactions and outlines future observational prospects.
conclusion: Self-interacting dark matter remains a viable hypothesis, with ongoing and future surveys expected to provide tighter constraints.

title: Nobel Lecture: Boltzmann Machines
authors: Geoffrey Hinton
abstract:
Author(s): Geoffrey Hinton

The 2024 Nobel Prize for Physics was shared by John Hopfield and Geoffrey Hinton. This paper is the text of the address given in conjunction with the award.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 030502] Published Mon Aug 25, 2025.
tldr: This is a Nobel lecture on Boltzmann machines, a classical machine learning model, with no direct connection to quantum information theory.
motivation: The paper presents the Nobel lecture by Geoffrey Hinton on Boltzmann machines, which are foundational in machine learning but not related to quantum information.
method: The lecture describes the concept and training of Boltzmann machines, a type of stochastic recurrent neural network.
result: The lecture summarizes the historical development and impact of Boltzmann machines in machine learning.
conclusion: Boltzmann machines are important for classical machine learning but have no direct relevance to quantum information theory.

title: Gas Bubble Dynamics
authors: Dominique Legendre And Roberto Zenit
abstract:
Author(s): Dominique Legendre and Roberto Zenit

The motion of gas bubbles in liquids plays a vital role in numerous natural, industrial, and everyday phenomena. Unlike solid particles, gas bubbles are nearly weightless and highly responsive to forces from the surrounding fluid. Their dynamics are affected by added mass acceleration and deformable surfaces, and also by interactions with turbulent flows, other bubbles, and walls, with liquid rheology and surfactants further influencing their behavior. This review examines the intricate behavior of noncondensable gas bubbles, highlighting key advances over the past 20 years. Key topics include turbulence, non-Newtonian fluids, and electrolytes, offering insights to enhance modeling and guide future research in two-phase flow systems.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 025001] Published Thu Apr 17, 2025.
tldr: This paper reviews the dynamics of gas bubbles in liquids, covering turbulence, non-Newtonian fluids, and electrolytes.
motivation: Understanding gas bubble dynamics is crucial for many natural and industrial processes, but the paper does not connect to quantum information or thermodynamics.
method: The paper is a review summarizing key advances over the past 20 years in bubble dynamics, including experimental and modeling approaches.
result: It highlights the effects of turbulence, non-Newtonian rheology, and surfactants on bubble behavior.
conclusion: The review provides insights for modeling two-phase flows but has no relevance to quantum information theory or related fields.

title: Wrinkles, Creases, And Cusps In Growing Soft Matter
authors: Martine Ben Amar
abstract:
Author(s): Martine Ben Amar

The buckling of a material surface subject to compression or growth is a ubiquitous phenomenon, arising in materials science contexts such as the swelling of gels as well as in biological contexts such as morphogenesis and embryogenesis. A complete understanding of the creases and sharp cusps that commonly accompany buckling requires nonlinear elasticity theory. This review presents a modern treatment of the Biot instability, integrating many standard techniques of nonlinear physics and solid mechanics, such as bifurcation theory, conformal mapping, and
[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 015004] Published Mon Feb 24, 2025.
tldr: This paper reviews nonlinear elasticity theory applied to buckling, creases, and cusps in growing soft matter, with no connection to quantum information or thermodynamics.
motivation: Understanding the formation of wrinkles, creases, and cusps in soft materials under compression or growth is important for materials science and biology.
method: The review integrates techniques from nonlinear physics and solid mechanics, including bifurcation theory, conformal mapping, and elliptic integrals.
result: It provides a modern treatment of the Biot instability and explains how nonlinear elasticity theory captures the observed patterns.
conclusion: The paper is a comprehensive review of buckling phenomena in soft matter, but it does not relate to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Propagation And Collisionless Damping Of Topologically-protected Surface Plasma Waves In Non-uniformly Magnetized Plasma Columns
authors: Roopendra Singh Rajawat And Gennady Shvets
abstract: Recent theoretical studies revealed the existence of topologically-protected surface plasma waves (TSPWs) in uniformly magnetized cold plasma columns. Reflections-free propagation of the TSPWs along arbitrarily-shaped plasma boundaries oriented perpendicularly to the magnetic field was shown to be preserved even when their collisionless damping by localized upper-hybrid resonances was accounted for. Here we extend this theory to the realistic case of three-dimensional magnetic field produced by finite-sized magnetic coils. We demonstrate that when TSPWs are launched in the direction of the decreasing magnetic field, they are collisionlessly absorbed within a highly localized (evanescent) region as they propagate away from the magnetic coil. We show that the resulting wave reflection can be negligible—in clear contrast with wave reflection from the corresponding evanescence regions of unmagnetized non-uniform plasmas.
tldr: This paper studies topologically-protected surface plasma waves in non-uniformly magnetized plasma columns, focusing on wave propagation and collisionless damping.
motivation: To extend the theory of topologically-protected surface plasma waves from uniformly magnetized to realistic three-dimensional magnetic fields, and to understand their absorption and reflection properties.
method: The authors theoretically analyze wave propagation in a cold plasma column with a non-uniform magnetic field produced by finite-sized coils, using a model that accounts for collisionless damping by upper-hybrid resonances.
result: They find that waves launched in the direction of decreasing magnetic field are collisionlessly absorbed in a localized evanescent region, with negligible reflection, contrasting with unmagnetized non-uniform plasmas.
conclusion: The study demonstrates robust, reflection-free absorption of topologically-protected surface plasma waves in realistic non-uniform magnetic fields, which may have implications for plasma heating and wave control.

title: Search For Decays Of The Higgs Boson Into Pair-produced Pseudoscalar Particles Decaying Into Τ + ...
authors: The ATLAS Collaboration
abstract: A search for a pair of low-mass pseudoscalars that promptly decay into -leptons is presented using 140 fb of proton–proton collision data at TeV centre-of-mass energy recorded with the ATLAS detector at the Large Hadron Collider. The result is used to place constraints on exotic decays of the Higgs boson into four -leptons, . This search focuses on events with either one or two -leptons decaying into hadrons and neutrinos, and the remaining three or two -leptons decaying into either electron or muon and neutrinos. No significant excess is observed above the expected Standard Model background and upper limits at the 95% confidence level on are set ranging from 0.06 to 0.23, depending on the mass ranging from 15 to 60 GeV.
tldr: This paper searches for exotic Higgs boson decays into pseudoscalar particles decaying into tau leptons using ATLAS data.
motivation: To probe beyond Standard Model physics through Higgs boson decays to new light particles.
method: Analyzes 140 fb^-1 of proton-proton collision data at 13 TeV, selecting events with tau leptons decaying hadronically or leptonically.
result: No significant excess over Standard Model background; sets 95% CL upper limits on branching ratio from 0.06 to 0.23 for pseudoscalar masses 15-60 GeV.
conclusion: The results constrain exotic Higgs decays but do not show evidence of new physics.

title: Orthogonal Phase Modulation And Lissajous Mode Decoupling In Light-induced Thermoelastic Spectroscopy For Real-time Multi-component Gas Sensing
authors: Hanxu Ma, Shunda Qiao, Ying He, Haiyue Sun And Yufei Ma
abstract: This paper proposed an optical detection mechanism that utilized orthogonal phase modulation (OPM) and Lissajous mode decoupling within a light-induced thermoelastic spectroscopy (LITES) sensor for the first time, enabling real-time multi-component gas sensing. By establishing a two-dimensional forced vibration model of a quartz tuning fork (QTF) under dual-path OPM, it revealed the vibration mode coupling mechanism induced by non-ideal phase and amplitude conditions, thereby providing a theoretical basis and optimization pathway for suppressing channel crosstalk. In the OPM-LITES sensor, two continuous-wave distributed feedback lasers were modulated by sinusoidal waves with the same frequency (f0/2, where f0 is the resonant frequency of the QTF) but a phase difference of 45°. The combined beam, after wavelength division multiplexing, co-excited the self-designed low-frequency QTF. The piezoelectric signal generated by the QTF underwent orthogonal demodulation via a lock-in amplifier (LIA). The concentration information for the two gases was independently retrieved from the decoupled X-component and Y-component of the LIA. Experimental results demonstrated that the OPM-LITES sensor exhibited excellent linear responses to both methane (CH4) and acetylene (C2H2), with average relative systematic errors of 0.54% and 0.79%, and maximum relative errors of 1.72% and 1.38%, respectively. Allan deviation analysis indicated that the minimum detection limits (MDLs) for CH4 and C2H2 reached 0.32 ppm and 0.29 ppm, with normalized noise-equivalent absorption coefficients of 5.09 × 10−9 cm−1·W·Hz−1/2 and 6.18 × 10−9 cm−1·W·Hz−1/2, respectively. This study not only provided a simple and efficient solution for real-time multi-component gas detection but also established a novel theoretical framework for mode decoupling and signal processing in spectroscopic sensing.
tldr: This paper presents a novel optical gas sensing technique using orthogonal phase modulation and Lissajous mode decoupling in light-induced thermoelastic spectroscopy for real-time multi-component gas detection.
motivation: Real-time multi-component gas sensing is important for environmental monitoring and industrial safety, but existing methods suffer from channel crosstalk and complexity.
method: Two continuous-wave lasers are modulated at the same frequency with a 45° phase difference, combined via wavelength division multiplexing, and co-excite a quartz tuning fork. The piezoelectric signal is orthogonally demodulated to decouple gas concentration information.

motivation: Antibiotic resistance is a growing crisis driven by selective pressure from antibiotics; new strategies to kill resistant bacteria without affecting susceptible ones are needed.
method: The authors designed a compound that remains harmless until activated by β-lactamase, which is produced by resistant bacteria, and then becomes a photosensitizer that generates reactive oxygen species upon light exposure.
